title: China targets fourfold boost in AI computing capacity by 2030 in major tech push
content:
China targets fourfold boost in AI computing capacity by 2030 in major tech push
The nation’s intelligent computing capacity hit 2,185 eflops at the end of June, up 177 per cent from a year earlier, according to MIIT
China plans to deploy artificial intelligence computing clusters containing 100,000 accelerator cards and sharply expand the country’s intelligent computing capacity over the next five years, as Beijing steps up investment in the infrastructure underpinning its AI ambitions.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), in a five-year industry plan released on Monday, set a target of 9,800 eflops of intelligent computing capacity by 2030, and called for 3.8 trillion yuan (US$532 billion) in cumulative information infrastructure investment over the 2026-2030 period.
The plan calls for the “orderly deployment” of intelligent computing clusters with 10,000 graphics processing cards or those using 100,000 or more cards, alongside inference computing facilities tailored to different applications. It also calls for greater efforts to adapt infrastructure to home-grown computing chips.
The targets extend a rapid expansion already under way. China’s intelligent computing capacity had reached 2,185 eflops – short for exa floating-point operations per second – by the end of June, up 177 per cent from a year earlier, and the country had built 52 intelligent computing facilities each equipped with more than 10,000 accelerator cards, according to MIIT.
That means China would need to more than quadruple the June level to reach the 2030 target. By the end of July, capacity had already risen to about 2,450 eflops, according to the National Data Administration, an agency overseen by the National Development and Reform Commission.
The expansion builds on the “East Data, West Computing” project launched in 2022, which seeks to shift power-intensive computing workloads from densely populated eastern regions towards western areas with cheaper land and abundant energy. China has since formed a network centred on eight national computing hubs, 10 data-centre clusters and three regions focused on coordinating computing facilities with power supplies.

report.summary: China plans to more than quadruple its AI computing capacity to 9,800 eflops by 2030, backed by huge infrastructure investment.
report.background: China’s new five-year plan from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology raises the country’s ambition for AI infrastructure amid intensifying US-China tech competition. Washington’s export controls have limited access to advanced accelerators from Nvidia and others, making domestically produced chips a priority. The plan extends the “East Data, West Computing” project launched in 2022, which routes energy-intensive workloads to western regions with cheaper power. China’s intelligent computing capacity reached 2,185 eflops by June, up 177 percent year on year, and over 2,450 eflops by July. Reaching the 2030 target of 9,800 eflops will require sustained, rapid construction of large-scale computing facilities.
key_points: The 2030 target of 9,800 eflops is more than four times China’s June capacity of 2,185 eflops, requiring an aggressive acceleration in data-center buildout. MIIT frames this as a national infrastructure push to keep pace with AI demand from industry, research, and public services.

The plan envisions RMB3.8 trillion (US$532 billion) in cumulative information infrastructure investment from 2026 to 2030, signaling a major state-guided spending wave aimed at computing, networking, and data storage that will support AI applications nationwide.

China will deploy intelligent computing clusters built with 10,000 or even 100,000-plus accelerator cards, while also adding inference facilities tailored to specific uses like autonomous driving and large language models rather than focusing only on AI training.

Infrastructure must adapt to home-grown computing chips, a response to US export restrictions on advanced semiconductors. This creates strong demand for domestic accelerators, software stacks, and developer tools that can substitute for Nvidia’s ecosystem and keep China’s AI sector resilient.

The plan builds on the existing 'East Data, West Computing' framework of eight national hubs, ten data-center clusters, and coordinated power-computing zones. This regional strategy aims to balance eastern data demand with western clean-energy supplies to make capacity expansion sustainable.
report.impact: For China’s AI industry, this plan signals that the government treats computing power as strategic national infrastructure and will fund its expansion through state-backed investment. Companies in the AI supply chain, especially domestic chip makers, cooling equipment providers, and energy suppliers, will see strong growth opportunities. Chinese developers and enterprises may need to increasingly optimize software for domestic accelerators rather than relying on Nvidia’s CUDA ecosystem. For ordinary users, expanded intelligent computing should mean better-performing consumer AI services, faster inference for chatbots and search, and lower costs as scale increases. The emphasis on western data centers also reshapes economic geography, bringing data-related jobs and renewable-energy projects to less-developed provinces.
report.tools: Developers and analysts watching this push should follow domestic AI accelerator ecosystems such as Huawei’s Ascend, Cambricon, and Biren, since the plan emphasizes local chip adaptation. Open-source frameworks like MindSpore (Huawei), PaddlePaddle (Baidu), and DeepSpark (open-source AI computing platform) provide practical entry points. For infrastructure updates, track MIIT and National Data Administration announcements, plus the 'East Data, West Computing' hub operators for deployment indicators.
